main_gate.title: Gwanghwamun: The Palace's Public Face
main_gate.subtitle: The ceremonial threshold between royal Seoul and the city outside.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Gwanghwamun is the main gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace and the place where the palace announces itself to the city. Its scale, central axis, and rebuilt watchtower frame the route toward the throne hall.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Pause before walking through and look at how the gate aligns with the courtyard sequence behind it. The palace experience is designed as a procession, moving from public space toward increasingly royal spaces.

ticket_booth.title: The Practical Gateway
ticket_booth.subtitle: A small stop that shapes the rhythm of the palace visit.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The ticket area is not historically grand, but it is where today's visitors shift from the city into the controlled palace grounds. It is also the right place to confirm admission rules before entering.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: This is a useful pause point. Check your ticket, water, and route before moving deeper into the palace where the courtyards become larger and less shaded.

geunjeongjeon.title: Geunjeongjeon: The Throne Hall
geunjeongjeon.subtitle: The formal heart of royal authority at Gyeongbokgung.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Geunjeongjeon was the main throne hall where kings held official ceremonies. Its name means industrious governance, connecting royal architecture to the ideal of disciplined rule.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: The wide stone courtyard is part of the experience. It makes the throne hall feel distant and elevated, reminding visitors that royal power was staged through space as much as through ceremony.

gyeonghoeru.title: Gyeonghoeru Pavilion and the Royal Pond
gyeonghoeru.subtitle: A banquet space built for ceremony, reflection, and spectacle.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Gyeonghoeru Pavilion was used for royal banquets and receiving foreign envoys. Resting on stone pillars above an artificial pond, it shows how architecture and landscape worked together in court culture.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Look at the pavilion's reflection and the openness of the pond. It is one of the palace's clearest examples of ceremonial space designed to impress guests.

national_palace_museum.title: National Palace Museum
national_palace_museum.subtitle: Objects, rituals, and everyday tools from the Joseon court.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The National Palace Museum preserves objects connected to royal life, state rituals, and Joseon visual culture. It helps turn the palace buildings into a fuller story of people and practices.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: If the palace grounds feel abstract, the museum adds detail. Look for objects that show how ceremony, scholarship, clothing, and administration shaped royal life.

heungnyemun.title: Heungnyemun: The Inner Approach
heungnyemun.subtitle: A gate that marks the transition into the palace core.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Heungnyemun is the second inner gate of Gyeongbokgung. Passing through it moves you closer to the ceremonial center and makes the palace sequence feel more controlled.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Notice the repeated gates and courtyards. The palace is not one building, but a series of thresholds that gradually prepare visitors for the throne hall.

sajeongjeon.title: Sajeongjeon: Daily Governance
sajeongjeon.subtitle: The king's executive office and a quieter center of decision-making.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Sajeongjeon was where the king met officials and handled daily state affairs. Its name suggests deep consideration before decisions, emphasizing governance as deliberation.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Compared with the throne hall, this space feels less theatrical. That contrast matters: ceremony projected authority, but rooms like this supported the everyday work of ruling.

gangnyeongjeon.title: Gangnyeongjeon: The King's Living Quarters
gangnyeongjeon.subtitle: A private royal space with a distinctive roofline.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Gangnyeongjeon served as the king's primary living and sleeping quarters. Its roof lacks the central ridge often seen elsewhere, a feature associated with the king's symbolic status.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: This area shifts the mood from public statecraft to private royal life. It helps show that the palace was both a government center and a residence.

gyotaejeon.title: Gyotaejeon: The Queen's Residence
gyotaejeon.subtitle: The center of the inner court and royal household life.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Gyotaejeon was the queen's primary living quarters and a key part of the inner court. It represents the domestic and political importance of royal women within palace life.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Look for the calmer scale and the relationship to the garden behind it. The residence connects directly to spaces designed for retreat, privacy, and display.

amisan.title: Amisan Garden
amisan.subtitle: A terraced garden built for the queen, famous for decorated chimneys.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Amisan is an artificial mound and terraced garden behind Gyotaejeon. Its decorated brick chimneys are treasured examples of palace craftsmanship and symbolic design.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: The garden is compact, but it rewards close looking. Notice the patterns and ornament on the chimneys rather than expecting a wide open park.

hyangwonjeong.title: Hyangwonjeong Pavilion
hyangwonjeong.subtitle: A picturesque island pavilion from the late Joseon period.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Hyangwonjeong is a two-story hexagonal pavilion built on an artificial island. Constructed in 1873, it reflects a later royal taste for scenic retreat within the palace grounds.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: This is one of the palace's most photographed views. The bridge, island, water, and pavilion create a composed landscape rather than a purely functional building.

national_folk_museum.title: National Folk Museum of Korea
national_folk_museum.subtitle: A museum about traditional Korean life beside the palace.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The National Folk Museum explains everyday Korean life through objects, rituals, and seasonal customs. It broadens the visit beyond kings and palaces.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: The building itself combines references to famous historical structures. It is a useful reminder that museums also communicate through architecture.

sinmumun.title: Sinmumun: The North Gate
sinmumun.subtitle: A palace exit facing the former presidential district.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Sinmumun is the northern gate of Gyeongbokgung. Today it connects the palace walk with the area near the Blue House, linking older royal authority with modern political history.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: If you exit here, the city context changes quickly. The gate is useful for understanding how the palace sits within Seoul's administrative landscape.

yeonchumun.title: Yeongchumun: The West Gate
yeonchumun.subtitle: A quieter side gate leading toward Seochon.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Yeongchumun, the Autumn Gate, served as a western entrance to the palace. It was associated with officials and daily movement rather than only grand ceremony.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Side gates show the palace as a working complex. They connect royal space to surrounding neighborhoods and practical routes through the city.

geonchunmun.title: Geonchunmun: The East Gate
geonchunmun.subtitle: A spring gate linked to royal-family movement.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Geonchunmun, the Spring Gate, is the eastern entrance. Historically, it was used by the royal family and their relatives.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: The name and placement make this gate feel less public than Gwanghwamun. It is a reminder that palace access was carefully organized by role and status.

sejong_statue.title: King Sejong in Gwanghwamun Square
sejong_statue.subtitle: A public monument to scholarship, governance, and Hangul.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: King Sejong is remembered as the creator of Hangul and one of Joseon's most important rulers. The statue places that legacy in the center of modern Seoul.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: The statue faces the city rather than hiding inside a palace. It turns royal memory into public civic space.

yi_sun_sin_statue.title: Admiral Yi Sun-sin
yi_sun_sin_statue.subtitle: A naval hero remembered in the center of Seoul.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Admiral Yi Sun-sin is celebrated for defending Korea during the Imjin War. His turtle ships and naval leadership became central symbols of resilience.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: The statue's posture and scale are deliberately heroic. It creates a strong visual counterpoint to the royal palace axis behind the square.

cheonggyecheon_plaza.title: Cheonggyecheon Stream Plaza
cheonggyecheon_plaza.subtitle: A restored stream that changed downtown Seoul.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Cheonggyecheon is a restored urban stream and public recreation space. Its plaza marks the start of an 11-kilometer corridor through the city.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: This area contrasts strongly with the palace. It shows modern Seoul's interest in reclaiming public space, water, and pedestrian routes.

gwanghwamun_station_9.title: Gwanghwamun Station Exit 9
gwanghwamun_station_9.subtitle: A transit threshold beneath the square.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Exit 9 connects the subway directly to Gwanghwamun Square. It is a practical gateway where underground Seoul meets the ceremonial city axis.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: This is often crowded. Use it as a reminder that Seoul's historical sites are embedded in a very active modern city.

sejong_center.title: Sejong Center for the Performing Arts
sejong_center.subtitle: A major cultural venue on Gwanghwamun Square.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The Sejong Center is one of Seoul's largest arts and cultural complexes. It extends the square's identity from political and royal history into performance and public culture.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Its scale and position make it part of the civic landscape. Around Gwanghwamun, culture, government, tourism, and transit all overlap.
